new_statements.quote: Gɩsɩɖa Anii has two tone levels, with both lexical and grammatical tone, though the grammatical tone is limited to only a few possible patterns (Morton, 2014). The mora is the Tone-bearing unit (tbu). The possible tone patterns on nouns with one- and two-syllable roots (the vast majority of non-compound nouns in the language) are given in (5), showing that the language contains all logically possible patterns, since contour tones are prohibited on a single tbu in the language as a whole. [...] In verbs, Gɩsɩɖa Anii has two lexical tone categories, H and L (though L is phonologically toneless). [...] the lexical H tone (when present, i.e. in H-toned stems) occurs on the second mora of the verb stem, and any following moras.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Anii (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements. This work adds that Anii is tonal (2 levels, lexical + grammatical tone, mora TBU) and is silent on word stress; nothing in it contradicts the catalog because the catalog records no placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Anii (Gɩsɩɖa/Bassila dialect) is described as a tone language: two tone levels (H, L), lexical and grammatical tone, mora as TBU, all four tone patterns (LL, LH, HL, HH) attested on disyllabic noun roots, verbs lexically H or toneless with lexical H realized on the second mora onward; grammatical H (e.g. far past) docks on the second mora, or the first if the second is already H. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the article and no statement about word stress, accent or non-tonal prominence is made; footnote 1 (p. 330) says every tone-bearing unit carries tone marking.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (no stress discussed at all)
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; for tone: contour tones prohibited on a single TBU; p. 335-336 notes a H tone on the second syllable of 'child' in the Balanka dialect as a dialect difference; p. 342: 'In terms of tone, then, Anii (or at least the Gɩsɩɖa dialect) seems to be more conservative than surrounding languages'.
new_statements.identity_note: Morton 2024 describes the Gɩsɩɖa dialect of Anii (the dialect of Bassila town, Benin, 'the only one that has been extensively studied', p. 328); the author explicitly hedges the tone characterization to 'Anii (or at least the Gɩsɩɖa dialect)' (p. 342) and notes tonal dialect differences (e.g. Balanka, pp. 335-336, Table 2).

audit.reasoning: The 'tonal' coding rests on the language's only grammar-length description, a 2014 dissertation whose second half is a dedicated tonology by the principal fieldworker; the deciding quotation is verbatim in the text we hold at the stated locators (abstract ii-iii, Ch.1 pp.17-18), and the negative claim (no Anii stress statement in 479 pp) was re-verified by a full-text search for stress/accent every 'stress/accent/prominence' hit. Glottolog's full 18-item bibliography and Morton's 2025 CV show no competing phonology, JIPA illustration, instrumental study or SIL sketch. Two open handouts downloaded now (ACAL 2013; 2017 workshop slides) restate the analysis and add free LL/LH/HL/HH noun-root patterns, which supports 'tonal' over pitch accent. Nothing found suggests a stress system; no reclassification or re-read needed.
